title: Penhold or shakehand: the two grips
seo_title: Penhold vs shakehand grip: the two ways to hold a bat
description: Penhold and shakehand grips explained: how each is held, Chinese and Japanese penhold, the reverse backhand, what the rules allow and which to learn.
summary: Almost every top player holds the bat as if shaking hands, but the pen grip still produces world-class players. Here is how the two grips work and which to start with.
key_points: Shakehand players hold the handle like a handshake and use one side of the bat for forehands and the other for backhands.
Penhold players grip the bat between thumb and forefinger, like a pen, with the other fingers behind the blade.
Japanese penhold blades suit playing with one side; Chinese penhold blades have short handles and let you use both.
The reverse penhold backhand, played with the back of the bat, is how modern penholders such as Félix Lebrun attack on both sides.
The rules allow any grip; most beginners should learn shakehand, but penhold is a sound choice if it feels natural.
body: There are two main ways to hold a table tennis bat. In the shakehand grip you wrap your hand round the handle as if shaking someone's hand, and play forehands with one side of the bat and backhands with the other. In the penhold grip you hold the bat between your thumb and forefinger, like a pen, with the other fingers curled behind the blade. Shakehand is by far the more common at every level, and it is the grip most coaches will teach you first. Penhold is less common but still wins world titles.

Hold the bat with the blade upright and the handle pointing at the floor, then take it as if you were shaking hands. Your middle, ring and little fingers wrap round the handle, your forefinger rests along the bottom edge of the blade on one side and your thumb sits on the blade on the other. Hold it gently: a tight grip stiffens the wrist and costs you feel.

With shakehand, the forehand and backhand use opposite sides of the bat. That is one reason the laws require one rubber to be black and the other a bright colour: your opponent can see which side you hit with. Our guide to [rubbers](/guide/table-tennis-rubbers-explained.html) explains why the two sides often play differently.

Shakehand blades come with several handle shapes. Butterfly describes its flared handle, which widens towards the end, as the shape "many players choose around the world", the straight handle as the one "the majority of choppers choose", and the anatomic handle, which bulges in the middle, as comfortable for beginners. Our guide to [blades](/guide/table-tennis-blades-explained.html) covers the differences.

Penholders pinch the handle between thumb and forefinger on the front of the bat and support the back of the blade with the other three fingers, either curled or spread out. Butterfly says its Japanese penhold handle allows "a wide variation of different wrist techniques", and the grip is at its best on the forehand and in short touch shots over the table. The traditional difficulty is the backhand: played with the same face as the forehand, it is hard to attack with.

Penhold blades are built differently from shakehand ones. Butterfly makes two penhold handles. Its Japanese penhold handle, it says, is "suited best for the sole use of one side of the blade", for players who hit every shot with the same face. Its Chinese penhold handles are "short and allow the use of both sides of the racket". As an example of the difference in length, the Chinese penhold version of Butterfly's Viscaria Super ALC has an 82mm handle, against 100mm for the flared shakehand Viscaria.

The modern answer to the penhold backhand is to turn the bat over and hit with the back. This reverse penhold backhand lets a penholder play a full topspin attack on the backhand side, as a shakehand player does. Wang Hao, the 2009 world champion and a three-time Olympic singles silver medallist, used the reverse side for almost all his backhands; when he joined the Chinese national team that approach was considered improper.

The best-known penholder today is France's [Félix Lebrun](/players/felix-lebrun.html), who took up the grip at four, inspired by Chen Jian, a Chinese penholder who trained in Montpellier. He plays with a reverse penhold backhand, won Olympic singles bronze at Paris 2024 aged 17, and was world No 3 in the [rankings](/rankings.html) of November 2026, the only penholder in the men's top 10.

He is an exception. At the 2022 World Team Championships, only two of the eight men's teams in the quarter-finals included a penholder, and 38 of the 40 players competing in those ties played shakehand.

The laws do not say how you must hold the bat. They only distinguish your racket hand, the one carrying the bat, from your free hand. A ball that hits your racket hand below the wrist counts as a good shot. Law 2.4.5 also leaves room for the way you hold it: the part of the blade nearest the handle, where your fingers grip, may be left uncovered or covered with any material, so you can cut the rubber back to suit your grip. Penholders who use only one face still have to cover or colour the other side: a side left without rubber must be matt and the right colour, and if you strike the ball with a side that does not meet the covering rules, you lose the point.

For most beginners, shakehand. It is easier to learn a strong backhand with it, almost all coaching and equipment is designed around it, and it is what you will see on most of the tables at your club. If you have played with a pen grip for years, or it feels far more natural, there is no reason to change: Lebrun shows the grip can reach the top. Choose one early, because switching later means relearning every stroke.

Whichever you pick, the next step is to think about how you want to play. Our guide to [playing styles](/guide/table-tennis-playing-styles.html) explains the options, and [what bat to buy](/guide/what-table-tennis-bat-to-buy.html) covers your first racket.
